title: Confessio Amantis
description: John Gower's English masterpiece: a collection of some 140 exemplary tales, mostly from Ovid, framed by the confession of the aging lover Amans to Genius, priest of Venus, who anatomizes the seven deadly sins as they corrupt love. Over 33,000 lines of octosyllabic couplets, with a Latin apparatus, it is the most substantial English poem of the century after the Canterbury Tales.
plot_or_argument: Amans, sick with unrequited love, prays to Venus and Cupid, who assign him Genius as confessor; book by book, Genius examines him on the sins of love, illustrating each with exemplary narratives — Florent and the loathly lady, Constance, Apollonius of Tyre, the tale of the Three Questions, and the story of Nebuchadnezzar's dream that closes the poem with a mirror for kings — until Venus cures him, shows him his aged face, and dismisses him 'John Gower' from love's service.
narrative_structure: An eight-book confessional frame (prologue, seven sins, epilogue) enclosing the exemplary tales, with the lover's cure as the poem's comic-pathetic resolution.
principal_characters: Amans (John Gower); Genius; Venus; Cupid; the exemplary figures of the tales
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets of great smoothness — the 'middle style' Gower made his own.
historical_context: Composed c. 1386–90 at the request of Richard II (first recension) and revised for Henry of Lancaster (c. 1392–93), in the period of the Peasants' Revolt and the king's fall; preserved in some fifty manuscripts and printed by Caxton (1483).
literary_significance: The classic English poem of the seven sins and the great 'mirror' collection of the Ricardian age; its tales (Apollonius, Florent) entered Shakespeare and the English narrative tradition.
attribution_notes: Gower's authorship secure; the poem's Latin verses name him throughout.
bibliographical_notes: Some fifty manuscripts. Standard edition: G. C. Macaulay, The English Works of John Gower, EETS ES 81–82 (1900–01).

title: Vox Clamantis
description: John Gower's Latin poem of some 10,000 elegiac couplets: an estates satire and dream vision in which the poet, during the Peasants' Revolt of 1381, sees the commons transformed into beasts and the social order inverted, then hears the estates — clergy, knights, peasants, merchants, lawyers — arraigned for their corruption. The great Latin poem of Ricardian England.
plot_or_argument: The first book (the Visio) allegorizes the 1381 rising as a bestial horde under Wat Tyler and Jack Straw ravaging the land; the remaining books survey each estate in turn, condemning clerical greed, knightly violence, peasant envy, and mercantile fraud, and close with a vision of the king (Richard II) as the realm's hope.
narrative_structure: Seven books: a dream-vision prologue on the revolt, then a systematic estates satire with the poet's own voice as its moral centre.
principal_characters: the Poet; the rebels (as beasts); the estates of society; Richard II
meter_and_prosody: Ovidian elegiac couplets, sustained with remarkable facility.
historical_context: Composed 1377–81, with the Visio added after the revolt of June 1381 (which Gower probably witnessed in London); revised in the 1390s; preserved in ten manuscripts, several with Gower's own annotations.
literary_significance: The most substantial Latin poem of fourteenth-century England and the classic estates satire of the Ricardian period; its account of the revolt is the age's defining literary image of 1381.
bibliographical_notes: Ten manuscripts. Standard edition: G. C. Macaulay, The Complete Works of John Gower, vol. 4 (1902); trans. E. W. Stockton (1962).

title: Testament of Love
description: Thomas Usk's allegorical prose apologia, written in the Tower of London before his execution in 1388: the imprisoned author, in Boethian dialogue with Love and her company, defends his political career, expounds free will and grace, and seeks the 'Margaret' of his devotion. For three centuries it was printed and read as Chaucer's.
plot_or_argument: The narrator, cast down by fortune and imprisoned, laments until the lady Love appears with her sisters; in three books she teaches him the nature of love and virtue, vindicates his service and his betrayals, and leads him through the doctrine of predestination and free will to the vision of the pearl of perfect bliss.
narrative_structure: Three books of Boethian consolation, with the acrostic of the opening chapters spelling the author's name and his lady's — 'MARGARETE OF VIRTW HAVE MERCI ON THIN USK'.
principal_characters: the Narrator (Usk); Love; Margaret (the pearl); Fortune; the Virtues
meter_and_prosody: Prose, richly Chaucerian in vocabulary and cadence.
historical_context: Composed 1384–88 in prison, in the factional struggles of Richard II's London (Usk had betrayed John of Northampton to Nicholas Brembre); the author's identity was recovered from the acrostic, overturning the Chaucerian attribution, only in the nineteenth century.
literary_significance: The first major prose work in the Chaucerian line and a unique document of the political prisoner's consolation; its false attribution shaped the early reception of Chaucer himself.
attribution_notes: Attribution to Usk secure from the acrostic and the records of his trial; previously attributed to Chaucer.
bibliographical_notes: BL Additional MS 24194; Thynne's 1532 Chaucer. Standard edition: G. W. Shawver, TEAMS (2002).

title: The Two Ways
alternative_titles: The Boke of the Two Ways
description: Sir John Clanvowe's devotional prose tract on the two ways of life and death — the narrow way of virtue and the broad way of the world — a Lollard-leaning meditation written in the circle of the 'Lollard knights' of Richard II's court, probably in 1391. It is the earliest prose work of the English reforming tradition by a lay courtier.
plot_or_argument: The tract expounds Christ's teaching of the two ways, contrasts the few who walk the narrow path with the many on the broad road to perdition, and anatomizes the sins of the world — pride, avarice, gluttony — with a particular Lollard sharpness against clerical wealth and display.
narrative_structure: A single homiletic meditation organized by the scriptural image of the two ways, with catalogue of sins and exhortation.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, earnest prose with scriptural quotation.
historical_context: Composed c. 1391 by the courtier-knight Clanvowe (d. October 1391), in the company of the Lollard knights at the court of Richard II; preserved in Bodleian MS Eng. th. c. 39 and later copies.
literary_significance: A principal document of the Lollard sensibility among the courtly elite and the earliest lay devotional prose of the Ricardian court.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Clanvowe in the manuscripts.
bibliographical_notes: Bodleian Library, MS Eng. th. c. 39. Standard edition: V. J. Scattergood, in The Works of Sir John Clanvowe (1975).

title: The Regiment of Princes
description: Thomas Hoccleve's mirror for princes of 5,463 lines in rhyme royal, addressed to the future Henry V and completed in 1411: an adaptation of the pseudo-Aristotelian Secretum Secretorum, Egidius Romanus's De Regimine Principum, and Jacobus de Cessolis's chess moralities, framed by the poet's famous dialogue with a beggar on poverty, patronage, and the life of the London clerk. The classic Lancastrian poem of good governance.
plot_or_argument: The sleepless poet, walking the fields of Westminster, meets an old beggar who catechizes him on the vanity of court service and the miseries of poverty; the dialogue then opens into the treatise proper — justice, mercy, patience, chastity, liberality, and the duties of the prince — closing with the counsel to the young Henry of Monmouth, prince of Wales.
narrative_structure: A mirror-for-princes in the frame of the poet's own autobiographical dialogue, the first English poem to make the writer's economic anxieties its prologue.
principal_characters: Hoccleve; the Beggar; Henry, Prince of Wales (addressee)
literary_form: mirror for princes in rhyme royal
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal stanzas of plain correctness, in Hoccleve's characteristic conversational register.
historical_context: Completed in 1411 by the Privy Seal clerk Hoccleve for the prince of Wales, on the eve of Agincourt; its portrait of the poor clerk's London is the most vivid account of bureaucratic life in the period; preserved in forty-three manuscripts.
literary_significance: The principal English mirror-for-princes of the fifteenth century and a landmark of autobiographical poetry; its beggar dialogue inaugurates the tradition of the poor poet's complaint.
attribution_notes: Hoccleve's authorship secure; he names himself throughout.
bibliographical_notes: Forty-three manuscripts. Standard edition: C. R. Blyth, TEAMS (1999).

title: The Series
description: Thomas Hoccleve's linked sequence of poems (c. 1419–21), beginning with the Complaint and the Dialogue with a Friend — the first extended account of mental illness in English poetry, describing his 'wylde infirmity' of 1416 — and continuing with the tale of the emperor Jereslaus's wife and the Learn to Die, translated from the Gesta Romanorum and Suso. The founding text of English confessional poetry.
plot_or_argument: The poet, unable to persuade the world of his recovered wits, complains of his illness and its social stigma; a Friend counsels and cajoles him back to writing; the sequence then proceeds through the exemplary tale of the empress and the treatise on dying, the poet's own voice threading the whole.
narrative_structure: A self-consciously linked series — complaint, dialogue, tale, and treatise — in which the frame of the poet's illness governs the exemplary matter.
principal_characters: Hoccleve; the Friend; the Emperor Jereslaus and his wife (tale)
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal throughout, with the prosimetric flourishes of the translated treatises.
historical_context: Composed c. 1419–21, after Hoccleve's breakdown of 1416, for Humphrey Duke of Gloucester among others; preserved in the holograph manuscripts (Durham, Cosin V.iii.9; BL Harley 4866) — the earliest English authorial manuscripts after Orm.
literary_significance: The first extended English poem of mental illness and recovery, and the first secular autobiography in English verse; its frankness has made it a touchstone of disability and confessional studies.
attribution_notes: Hoccleve's authorship secure; parts survive in his own hand.
bibliographical_notes: Durham, Cosin MS V.iii.9; BL Harley MS 4866. Standard edition: J. J. Thompson et al., in Thomas Hoccleve's 'Series' (1992–2002).

title: Troy Book
description: John Lydgate's vast verse translation (over 30,000 lines) of Guido delle Colonne's Historia destructionis Troiae, commissioned by Henry V in 1412 and completed in 1420: the full Trojan story retold as a mirror of chivalry, kingship, and tragedy. The most ambitious poem of the fifteenth century and the foundation of Lydgate's fame.
plot_or_argument: From Jason and the golden fleece through the rape of Helen and the ten years' war to the fall of Troy and the wanderings of the Greeks, the poem recounts the Trojan matter at length, moralizing throughout on pride, treason, and the fickleness of fortune, with Hector as its pattern of knighthood.
narrative_structure: Five books following Guido's divisions, with prologue and envoy to Henry V; set-piece descriptions, speeches, and moral digressions throughout.
principal_characters: Hector; Achilles; Priam; Paris; Helen; Troilus; Ulysses; Agamemnon
meter_and_prosody: Decasyllabic couplets in the 'Lydgate line', frequently headless, with aureate diction.
historical_context: Commissioned by Henry, Prince of Wales, in 1412, completed in 1420, and dedicated to the king after Agincourt; its Troy matter spoke to Lancastrian imperial ambition; printed by Pynson (1513) and widely read into the sixteenth century.
literary_significance: The fullest English Troy narrative and the great monument of Lancastrian literary patronage; it made Lydgate the laureate of the fifteenth century and fed the Tudor cult of Troy.
bibliographical_notes: Some twenty manuscripts. Standard edition: H. Bergen, EETS ES 97, 103, 106, 126 (1906–35).

title: The Siege of Thebes
description: John Lydgate's continuation of the Canterbury Tales (c. 1420–22), presented as the monk of Bury's own tale on the return journey from Canterbury: the story of Thebes from the founding of the city by Cadmus through the tragedy of Oedipus, the war of the Seven, and the deaths of the Theban and Argive heroes. Its frame makes it the first great poem of the Chaucerian succession.
plot_or_argument: Joining the pilgrims at Canterbury, Lydgate's monk tells the Theban story: Oedipus's parricide and incest, the quarrel of his sons Eteocles and Polynices, the expedition of the Seven against Thebes, the duel of the brothers, and the funeral of the heroes — a chain of fortune's falls moralized throughout.
narrative_structure: A Chaucerian frame (the return-journey tale) enclosing the three-part Theban narrative, with the 'tragedy' of Fortune as its moral armature.
principal_characters: the Monk of Bury (narrator); Oedipus; Eteocles; Polynices; Tydeus; Adrastus; Creon
literary_form: verse narrative in couplets (framed as Canterbury tale)
meter_and_prosody: Decasyllabic couplets in the Lydgate manner.
historical_context: Composed c. 1420–22, in direct response to Chaucer's Knight's Tale (the Theban matter of its background), and copied with the Canterbury Tales in many manuscripts; printed by Wynkyn de Worde (1497).
literary_significance: The first great act of Chaucerian imitation: by writing himself into the pilgrimage, Lydgate claimed Chaucer's mantle and set the pattern for the fifteenth-century canon of English poetry.
bibliographical_notes: Some thirty manuscripts, often with the Canterbury Tales. Standard edition: A. Erdmann, EETS ES 108, 125 (1911–30).

title: Fall of Princes
description: John Lydgate's monumental translation (over 36,000 lines) of Boccaccio's De Casibus Virorum Illustrium, commissioned by Humphrey Duke of Gloucester and completed in 1438: a procession of the falls of princes from Adam to King John of France, moralized by the ghostly narrator Boccaccio himself. The encyclopedic English 'tragedy' of fortune, and the ancestor of the Mirror for Magistrates.
plot_or_argument: The poet, in a Boethian frame, receives the sorrowing Boccaccio, who recounts example after example of greatness overthrown — Nimrod, Saul, Priam, Alexander, Caesar, Nero, Arthur, and the modern princes — each tale closing with the moral of fortune's wheel; the work ends with the falls of the French and English kings and a defense of poetry itself.
narrative_structure: Nine books of exemplary falls within the dream-vision frame, with the envoy to Duke Humphrey as its patronage climax.
principal_characters: Lydgate (dreamer); Boccaccio (narrator); the fallen princes of history
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal stanzas with prose links, aureate and copious.
historical_context: Commissioned by Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, in 1431 and completed in 1438, during the wars in France and the king's minority; printed by Pynson (1494) and continuously read; the Mirror for Magistrates (1559) descends directly from it.
literary_significance: The great English poem of the falls of princes and the conduit by which Boccaccio's tragic vision became the Tudor theory of tragedy; its influence on the Elizabethan stage is direct.
bibliographical_notes: Some forty manuscripts. Standard edition: H. Bergen, EETS ES 121–124 (1924–27).

title: The Temple of Glas
description: John Lydgate's early dream vision (1,403 lines in rhyme royal, c. 1400–05): the dreamer, enclosed in a glass temple of Venus, overhears the complaint of a lady bound by an unwanted marriage and the answering lament of her true lover, until the goddess unites them. The most accomplished of Lydgate's courtly poems and the first printed by Caxton.
plot_or_argument: The dreamer finds himself before a temple of glass whose walls depict famous lovers; within, the lady laments her forced betrothal and the knight his despair; Venus, appealed to by both, grants them one another, and the dreamer wakes to write his vision for his own lady.
narrative_structure: A courtly dream vision in the Chaucerian manner (House of Fame, Parliament of Fowls), with the double complaint as its centre.
principal_characters: the Dreamer; the Lady; her Lover; Venus
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal stanzas with the early Lydgate line's characteristic fluency.
historical_context: Composed c. 1400–05, early in Lydgate's career, perhaps for a marriage occasion; widely copied and printed — it was among the first poems Caxton printed at Westminster (1477).
literary_significance: The finest of Lydgate's courtly visions and a key text of the early Chaucerian tradition; its printing history marks the beginning of the English poetry market.
attribution_notes: Lydgate's authorship secure (named in the envoy).
bibliographical_notes: Some thirty manuscripts. Standard edition: J. A. Mitchell, TEAMS (2007).

title: Le Morte Darthur
alternative_titles: The Whole Book of King Arthur and of His Noble Knights of the Round Table
description: Sir Thomas Malory's great prose compilation of the Arthurian legend, completed in prison in 1469–70 and printed by Caxton in 1485: from the sword in the stone and the winning of Guinevere, through the adventures of Lancelot, Tristram, and the Grail quest, to the breaking of the Round Table, the last battle, and Arthur's passing to Avalon. The definitive English Arthurian book.
plot_or_argument: Malory weaves the French prose cycles and English alliterative poems into a single tragic narrative: Arthur's accession and marriage, the founding of the Round Table, the quests and loves of its knights, the Grail quest that divides the fellowship, the adultery of Lancelot and Guinevere, and the final war against Mordred in which Arthur falls — his body borne to Avalon, his epitaph 'Rex quondam Rexque futurus'.
narrative_structure: Eight books (Caxton's twenty-one divisions) of interlaced adventure compressed into linear narrative, with the Grail and the Lancelot-Guinevere tragedy as the arcs that break the fellowship.
principal_characters: Arthur; Lancelot; Guinevere; Gawain; Tristram; Isolde; Galahad; Merlin; Morgan le Fay; Mordred
meter_and_prosody: Prose: paratactic, ritual, and rhythmic, with the famous Malorian cadence of balanced clauses and repeated key words.
historical_context: Completed by the 'knight prisoner' Thomas Malory in the ninth year of Edward IV (1469–70), during the Wars of the Roses; Caxton's 1485 print fixed the text for three centuries until the discovery of the Winchester manuscript (1934) revealed the pre-print version.
literary_significance: The summit of English Arthurian literature and the conduit of the Arthurian story to Spenser, Tennyson, and the modern novel; its vision of chivalry — at once idealized and doomed — is the period's most enduring legacy.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Sir Thomas Malory of Newbold Revel (d. 1471) on the evidence of the colophons; the identification is widely though not universally accepted.
bibliographical_notes: Winchester manuscript (BL Additional MS 59678); Caxton's print (1485). Standard edition: E. Vinaver, 3rd edn rev. P. J. C. Field (1990).

title: Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye
alternative_titles: The Recuyell of the Histories of Troy
description: William Caxton's translation of Raoul Lefèvre's French Recueil des histoires de Troyes, begun in Bruges in 1468 and completed in Cologne in 1471, and printed by Caxton at Bruges in 1473–74 as the first book printed in English. A courtly Troy compilation made for the Burgundian duchess Margaret of York, it inaugurated both Caxton's career and the English printed book.
plot_or_argument: The compilation recounts the deeds of Hercules and the first destruction of Troy, then the rebuilding of the city under Priam and the second war — the rape of Helen, the battles before Troy, the deaths of Hector and Achilles, and the fall of the city through the wooden horse.
narrative_structure: Three books in Lefèvre's arrangement, translated in full, with Caxton's prologue and epilogue recording the circumstances of its making.
principal_characters: Hercules; Jason; Priam; Hector; Achilles; Paris; Helen; Ulysses
meter_and_prosody: Prose: Caxton's early style, French-inflected and courtly, before his London plainness matured.
historical_context: Begun in Bruges in 1468 for Margaret of York, sister of Edward IV, and printed at Bruges c. 1473–74 — the first English printed book; Caxton's famous prologue records his despair over the labour of translation and the duchess's command to finish.
literary_significance: The first book printed in English and the founding text of the English print tradition; its Troy matter carried the medieval romance of antiquity into the print era.
attribution_notes: Caxton's authorship of the translation and printing is documented in his own prologue and epilogue.
bibliographical_notes: Caxton's Bruges print (c. 1473–74). Standard edition: H. O. Sommer, 2 vols (1894).

title: The Golden Legend
description: William Caxton's translation of Jacobus de Voragine's Legenda Aurea, printed at Westminster in 1483: the great medieval collection of saints' lives and feasts of the church year, in nearly 450 leaves and the first English printing of the work. It became the standard English legendary for a century, reprinted repeatedly into the 1520s.
plot_or_argument: Following the church year, the collection narrates the lives and martyrdoms of the saints — from St Andrew through the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins — with the great feasts (Advent, Christmas, Passiontide) expounded and the legends moralized for the reader's instruction.
narrative_structure: A calendrical legendary in the Voragine tradition, with Caxton's additions (including lives of English saints) and his prologue explaining the work's purpose.
meter_and_prosody: Prose: Caxton's mature plain style at its most ample.
historical_context: Translated by Caxton from French and Latin sources and printed at Westminster in 1483, in the orthodox devotional market of pre-Reformation England; nine editions appeared by 1527, before the Reformation ended the cult of the saints it served.
literary_significance: The great bestseller of Caxton's press and the principal English channel of the Legenda Aurea; its saints' lives nourished English devotional reading into the sixteenth century.
attribution_notes: Caxton's translation is documented in his own prologue.
bibliographical_notes: Caxton's print (1483). Standard edition: M. Taguchi, J. Scahill, and S. Tokunaga, EETS OS 355 (2020).

title: Reynard the Fox
alternative_titles: The History of Reynard the Fox
The Historye of Reynart the Foxe
description: William Caxton's translation of the Dutch prose Reinaert de Vos, printed at Westminster in 1481: the beast epic of the fox Reynard, whose crimes are arraigned at the court of King Noble the lion, and whose cunning turns every accusation — and his own execution — into the ruin of his accusers. Caxton's print brought the European Reynard tradition to English readers and printers alike.
plot_or_argument: Summoned to the lion's court to answer the complaints of the wolf Isengrim, the bear Bruin, and the other beasts, Reynard tricks each accuser in turn, confesses to save his neck, and is sent on pilgrimage only to murder his escort; his enemies' heads decorate his house, and the lion makes him his counsellor — the trickster triumphant.
narrative_structure: A beast epic in episodic form: arraignment, defence, confession, and triumph, in the framework of the animals' court.
principal_characters: Reynard the Fox; King Noble the Lion; Isengrim the Wolf; Bruin the Bear; Tibert the Cat; Chanticleer the Cock
meter_and_prosody: Prose: Caxton's plain, lively narrative style at its best.
historical_context: Translated by Caxton from the Dutch and printed in 1481, in the same year as his Godfrey of Boulogne; it fed a long English print tradition of Reynard editions and the beast satire of the sixteenth century.
literary_significance: The classic English Reynard and the ancestor of the beast satire that runs through Spenser's Mother Hubberds Tale to the seventeenth-century Reynard reprints; a landmark of Caxton's publishing program.
attribution_notes: Caxton's translation documented in his own colophon.
bibliographical_notes: Caxton's print (1481). Standard edition: N. F. Blake, EETS OS 263 (1970).
